core_intuitions: A scaling ladder is a MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT: hold the entire recipe frozen (tokenizer, data order, optimizer, WSD schedule, arch stack) and vary ONLY N and D. The fit is trustworthy only because everything you are not varying is invariant; drift turns a law-fit into a noise-fit (the Kaplan confound).

The sweep must probe the N-D plane in BOTH directions. IsoFLOP slices all lie on constant-6ND diagonals - a degenerate direction that cannot separate alpha from beta in the additive form; a few off-diagonal fixed-model points (cheap rungs pushed to very low and very high tokens/param) break the degeneracy and pin the exponents.

Fit on NON-EMBEDDING parameters. At vocab 32,768 the tied 16.8M embedding is FOUR TIMES the rest of the 4M rung; counting it swamps the depth-driven capacity signal and corrupts the exponent. The 6ND FLOP rule counts non-embedding N too.

The loss EXTRAPOLATES but the constants DO NOT. The additive surface is nearly flat near the optimum, so E, A, B are strongly correlated and only weakly identified (A comes out 3-4x off, E wanders half a nat); yet because the target sits only 0.28 decades past the top rung, the compensating errors cancel and the predicted loss lands within ~0.1 nat. Validate by extrapolation, never by admiring the raw constants.

Compute-optimal is not deployment-optimal. For the SAME FLOP budget, a smaller over-trained model (85M @ 200 tok/param) matches the loss of a larger compute-optimal one (190M @ 40 tok/param) to within ~0.01 nat, yet costs ~55% less on EVERY future forward pass. Minimize lifetime compute 6*N*D_train (once) + 2*N*D_infer (forever), not just training compute.

Two methods, one answer: the parametric L(N,D) fit and Chinchilla's IsoFLOP-parabola method agree on an allocation exponent a ~= 0.5 (N* and D* grow roughly together) - but IsoFLOP needs a DENSE slice (6+ models bracketing the vertex), so the 4-rung ladder pins the allocation via the parametric fit and uses coarse valleys only as a sanity check.

new_figures.name: ladder-sweep-nd-plane
new_figures.concept: The whole ladder as a measurement instrument laid out on the N-D plane: fixed-N rung columns, constant-6ND IsoFLOP diagonals, off-diagonal points that break the degeneracy, and the short honest extrapolation reach to the target.
new_figures.rationale: This is the operational heart of the chapter and its single biggest visual gap. The prose describes a 'hybrid grid' (IsoFLOP backbone + off-diagonal fixed-model points) and repeatedly invokes the degeneracy of constant-6ND lines, but the reader has no picture of WHY those two run families are complementary. One figure on the log-log N-D plane makes it click at once: IsoFLOP points slide along a diagonal (a degenerate direction), off-diagonal points reach off it, and the target sits just 0.28 decades past the top rung so the law barely has to reach. Non-overlapping with the theory chapter's generic IsoFLOP-valley figure - this is the concrete Stack ladder as a designed experiment.
new_figures.placement: Designing the sweep: an IsoFLOP backbone plus off-diagonal points
new_figures.brief: A single static log-log scatter on the N-D plane. X-axis: 'non-embedding parameters N (log)', ticks at the four rungs S1 ~3.9M, S2 ~9.2M, S3 ~18.8M, S4 ~44M, plus a dashed tick at the target ~84.5M sitting just a short step (0.28 decades) to the right of S4. Y-axis: 'training tokens D (log)'. Draw four faint PARALLEL diagonals of slope -1 (since log D = log C - log 6 - log N), one per compute budget C in {6e15, 1.5e16, 4e16, 1e17}, labeled collectively 'lines of constant compute (IsoFLOP): 6ND = C' with each line tagged by its C. Place the IsoFLOP-BACKBONE points (filled dots) where each budget diagonal crosses a rung column - i.e. the ISO list in the chapter: 6e15 at S1,S2; 1.5e16 at S1,S2,S3; 4e16 at S1,S2,S3; 1e17 at S2,S3,S4. Place the OFF-DIAGONAL fixed-model points (open/hollow markers of a second accent) as extra dots on the rung columns at very low and very high tokens/param: S1,S2,S3 at ~12 tok/param (low), S4 at ~20, and S1 at ~300 and S2 at ~120 (high) - these lie clearly OFF the backbone diagonals. Add two key annotations with leader lines: (1) pointing along a diagonal, 'IsoFLOP slices lie on a constant-6ND line - a degenerate direction: cannot separate alpha from beta'; (2) pointing at a high/low off-diagonal pair, 'off-diagonal points (cheap rungs pushed to very few / very many tokens) break the degeneracy and pin the exponents'. Draw a short arrow from the S4 cluster to the dashed target column: 'extrapolate 44M -> 84.5M (0.28 decades - a short, honest reach)'. Optionally show faint diagonal guide lines for tokens/param = 20 and 200 for orientation. Keep to ~17 plotted points total, all legible, no overlapping labels. Theme-safe: theme ink for axes/text, one accent for backbone dots + diagonals, a second accent for the off-diagonal markers, a dashed neutral for the target column. Everything inside the viewBox; clear reading order left-to-right, bottom-to-top.
new_figures._note: log-log plane; IsoFLOP diagonals have slope -1; two marker families must be visually distinct.

new_figures.name: loss-extrapolates-constants-dont
new_figures.concept: Many different (E,A,B) triples fit the same 17 ladder points almost equally well - their floors and amplitudes disagree wildly - yet all of them land inside a narrow ~0.1-nat band at the target, so the PREDICTION is trustworthy even though the CONSTANTS are not.
new_figures.rationale: This is the chapter's signature epistemic lesson and its most counterintuitive claim ('if your colleague's fit reports different constants, neither of you is wrong'). It is almost impossible to grasp from prose alone but immediate as a picture: a fan of curves that are far apart in their tails/floors yet nearly coincident across the measured-to-target window. It directly teaches the takeaway 'validate by extrapolation, never by admiring the raw constants' and explains why the ~0.1-nat band is exactly enough to catch a broken run (0.3+ nats off) but useless for splitting hairs. Unique to this chapter.
new_figures.placement: Read the fit honestly: the loss extrapolates, the constants do not
new_figures.brief: A static loss-vs-tokens plot at the TARGET model size. X-axis: 'training tokens D (log), at N = 84.5M'; Y-axis: 'loss L (nats/token)'. Shade a vertical 'MEASURED LADDER region' band on the left where the ladder's D values live, and mark a scatter of a handful of measured points inside it. Draw 3-4 FITTED curves of the Chinchilla form L = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta, each from a different noise-seed fit (annotate each with schematic, deliberately-DIFFERENT constants, e.g. 'fit A: E~2.4, A~480' vs 'fit B: E~2.9, A~120' - these illustrate the 3-4x swing the chapter reports; invent no precise numbers beyond the chapter's stated ranges). Critically: give each curve its OWN irreducible-floor dashed horizontal asymptote at a DIFFERENT height (the E's disagree by ~half a nat) - draw these faint dashed floors so the reader sees the constants genuinely diverge. Yet in the measured region AND out to the target the curves should nearly overlap. Mark two vertical target lines at 20 tok/param (~D=1.7B, L~3.15) and 200 tok/param (~D=16.9B, L~2.95). At each target line, draw a small vertical bracket spanning where the curves land, labeled '+/-0.1 nat band'. Between the two target lines draw a bracket for the ~0.20-nat over-training gain, labeled 'this DIFFERENCE is well-pinned (depends on exponents, not the loose floor)'. Headline annotation across the top: 'the constants disagree; the prediction agrees'. Small footer: 'a broken run misses by 0.3+ nats - caught on hour two'. Theme-safe: theme ink for axes; the fan of fitted curves in one accent family (slightly varied), the divergent floors as faint dashed neutral lines, the target brackets in a second accent. Legible in both themes; no overlapping labels; all inside viewBox.
new_figures._note: The pedagogical trick is: floors E fan apart, curves converge in the measured-to-target window.

new_figures.name: overtrain-vs-compute-optimal-headtohead
new_figures.concept: Two ways to spend the SAME ~8.6e18 training FLOPs: a compute-optimal 190M @ 7.5B tokens vs the plan's over-trained 85M @ 16.9B tokens. Near-identical loss, but the over-trained model is less than half the size and ~55% cheaper on every inference forever.
new_figures.rationale: This is the chapter's climax - the counterintuitive decision to deliberately over-train an order of magnitude past compute-optimal - and the interview-corner question turns on it. The chapter presents it as a two-row table; a head-to-head infographic makes the trade viscerally clear: same FLOP budget, imperceptible ~0.01-nat loss difference, but a permanent halving of inference cost. It frames the lifetime-compute idea (pay training once, collect inference savings forever) that a static table cannot dramatize. Distinct from the theory chapter's generic 'sliding optimum' figure: this is the concrete same-budget head-to-head with the ladder's own numbers.
new_figures.brief: A static side-by-side comparison of two runs that consume the SAME training budget. Top strip: a single bar labeled 'same training compute: 6ND ~= 8.6e18 FLOPs' spanning the width, emphasizing both choices spend equally. Two panels below, LEFT 'compute-optimal' and RIGHT 'our choice (over-trained)'. In each panel show the model as a block whose two dimensions encode N and D: LEFT = wide-and-short (N=190M large, D=7.5B fewer tokens, 40 tok/param); RIGHT = narrow-and-tall (N=85M small, D=16.9B more tokens, 200 tok/param) - the equal-area motif (N x D constant) visually says 'same 6ND'. Under each, a loss readout: LEFT 'train loss ~2.94', RIGHT 'train loss ~2.95', with a connecting brace 'delta ~= 0.01 nat - imperceptible in generated text'. Below that, an INFERENCE-COST comparison: two horizontal bars proportional to 2N (cost per token), LEFT bar for 190M clearly ~2.2x longer than RIGHT bar for 85M, annotated 'every future forward pass ~55% cheaper - permanently (memory, latency, KV cache too)'. A caption strip tying it together: 'lifetime compute = 6*N*D_train (train ONCE) + 2*N*D_infer (serve FOREVER)'; and a one-liner 'pay the extra training tokens once; collect the inference savings on every request'. Add a small robustness note badge: 'loss LEVELS carry +/-0.1 nat; the ~0.01-nat penalty and 0.45x size ratio do NOT - they are set by the exponents + the fixed FLOP constraint'. Numbers used (190M, 7.5B, 40; 85M, 16.9B, 200; ~2.94/~2.95; 8.6e18; ~55%) are all stated in the chapter - use only these. Theme-safe: one accent for the train term, a second for the serve/inference term, theme ink for text; both panels balanced and legible in light and dark; no overlaps; all within viewBox.
new_figures._note: The equal-area (N x D) block motif is the crux: two very different shapes, same training FLOPs.

new_figures.name: nonembed-vs-embedding-trap
new_figures.concept: At the small rungs the fixed 16.8M tied embedding table dwarfs the transformer blocks - four times the entire rest of the 4M rung - so fitting on TOTAL parameters lets a per-token-constant embedding swamp the depth-driven capacity signal and corrupt the exponent.
new_figures.rationale: The chapter flags this as 'a trap unique to small models that the frontier literature glosses over' and it is the reason every N in the chapter is a non-embedding count. It is a small but genuinely load-bearing intuition (get it wrong and the whole exponent rotates), and it is inherently visual: a stacked bar across the rungs where the embedding slab stays fixed while the block slab grows shows instantly why total-param fits are poisoned at this scale. Cheap, foundational, and unique to the small-model regime this chapter lives in.
new_figures.placement: The embedding subtlety you must not ignore
new_figures.brief: A static stacked-bar chart across the four rungs plus the target. X-axis: rungs S1 (3.9M blocks), S2 (9.2M), S3 (18.8M), S4 (44M), target (84.5M) - these are the NON-EMBEDDING counts. Each bar is stacked into two segments: a FIXED embedding slab of 16.8M (identical height on every bar - draw a faint horizontal guide line at 16.8M so the constancy is obvious) and a GROWING blocks slab equal to the rung's non-embedding N. Y-axis: 'parameters (M)'. The punchline reads off the S1 bar: annotate 'at the 4M rung the embedding (16.8M) is ~4x the entire rest of the model' with the ratio called out. Show that the embedding fraction SHRINKS as rungs grow (annotate S1 'embedding = 81% of total' schematic vs target 'embedding = 17% of total' - these follow from 16.8M/(16.8M+N); keep them as illustrative round percentages consistent with the chapter's numbers). Add two labels distinguishing the roles: on the embedding slab 'fixed work per token, no depth-driven capacity scaling'; on the blocks slab 'the sequence-mixing + feature-transform params the 6ND rule counts'. Bottom caption: 'fit the law on NON-EMBEDDING N (the blocks slab); counting the embedding corrupts the exponent'. Numbers used (16.8M embedding, rung non-embed counts, target 84.5M, ~4x) are all from the chapter. Theme-safe: one accent (muted) for the embedding slab, a second (stronger) for the blocks slab, theme ink for text and the 16.8M guide line; legible in both themes; no overlapping labels; all within viewBox.
new_figures._note: The fixed-height embedding slab beside a growing blocks slab is the whole point - keep the 16.8M guide line prominent.

summary: This capstone chapter has NO figures yet and is concept-rich exactly where intuition needs pictures. I avoid duplicating the theory chapter's (03-pretraining/04) generic IsoFLOP-valley and inference-aware-overtraining figures, and instead specify four figures unique to the applied 'fit your own law' story. Priority-1: ladder-sweep-nd-plane (the ladder as a designed experiment on the log-log N-D plane - fixed-N rung columns, constant-6ND IsoFLOP diagonals, off-diagonal points that break the alpha/beta degeneracy, and the short 0.28-decade extrapolation to the target), and loss-extrapolates-constants-dont (the chapter's signature epistemic lesson - a fan of fitted curves whose floors E disagree by half a nat yet converge into a ~0.1-nat band at the target). Priority-2: overtrain-vs-compute-optimal-headtohead (the climax decision - same 8.6e18 FLOPs, ~0.01-nat loss difference, ~55% permanent inference cut, framed by lifetime compute 6ND_train + 2ND_infer). Priority-3: nonembed-vs-embedding-trap (a stacked bar showing the fixed 16.8M embedding slab dwarfing the small rungs, the reason every N is a non-embedding count). All are static - a single frame conveys each fully; no animation is essential here. All briefs stay theme-safe and use only numbers stated in the chapter.
